# rqrr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rqrr/

## Expand description

Find and read QR-Codes

This crates exports functions and types that can be used to search for QR-Codes in images and decode them.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The most basic usage is shown below:

```
use image;
// Load on image to search, convert it to grayscale
let img = image::open("tests/data/github.gif")?.to_luma8();
// Prepare for detection
let mut img = rqrr::PreparedImage::prepare(img);
// Search for grids, without decoding
let grids = img.detect_grids();
assert_eq!(grids.len(), 1);
// Decode the grid
let (meta, content) = grids[0].decode()?;
assert_eq!(meta.ecc_level, 0);
assert_eq!(content, "https://github.com/WanzenBug/rqrr");
```
If you have some other form of picture storage, you can use
[ PreparedImage::prepare_from_*](https://docs.rs/struct.PreparedImage.html). This allows
you to define your own source for images.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Grid](https://docs.rs/struct.Grid.html)
- Wrapper around any grid that can be interpreted as a QR code
- [Meta](https://docs.rs/struct.MetaData.html)- Data
- MetaData for a QR grid
- [Mirrored](https://docs.rs/struct.MirroredGrid.html)- Grid
- Mirrored grid, switching x and y coordinates
- [Point](https://docs.rs/struct.Point.html)
- A simple point in (some) space
- [Prepared](https://docs.rs/struct.PreparedImage.html)- Image
- An black-and-white image that can be mutated on search for QR codes
- [RawData](https://docs.rs/struct.RawData.html)
- The bit stream contained in the QR Code
- [Simple](https://docs.rs/struct.SimpleGrid.html)- Grid
- A basic GridImage that can be generated from a given function.
- [Version](https://docs.rs/struct.Version.html)
- Version of a QR Code which determines its size

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [DeQR](https://docs.rs/enum.DeQRError.html)- Error
- Possible errors that can happen during decoding

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [BitGrid](https://docs.rs/trait.BitGrid.html)
- A grid that contains exactly one QR code square.

## Expand description

This crates exports functions and types that can be used to search for QR-Codes in images and decode them.

```

# rust-qr-reader - Find and read QR-Codes

This crates exports functions and types that can be used to search for QR-Codes in images and decode them.

## Usage

The most basic usage is shown below:

```
use image;
use rqrr;
let img = open?.to_luma;
// Prepare for detection
let mut img = prepare;
// Search for grids, without decoding
let grids = img.detect_grids;
assert_eq!;
// Decode the grid
let  = grids.decode?;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
For more information visit [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/rqrr/)

# g2p - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/g2p/^1.0/

## Expand description

This crate can generate types that implement fast finite field arithmetic.

Many error correcting codes rely on some form of finite field of the form GF(2^p), where p is relatively small. Similarly some cryptographic algorithms such as AES use finite field arithmetic.

While addition and subtraction can be done quickly using just a simple XOR, multiplication is more involved. To speed things up, you can use a precomputed table. Typically this table is just copied into the source code directly.

Using this crate, you can have the benefits in speed of precomputed table, without the need to create your own type with custom multiplication and division implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)WARNING

The types generated by this library are probably not suitable for cryptographic purposes, as multiplication is not guaranteed to be constant time.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

The implementation was tested for finite fields up to 2^17 in size, which compiles reasonably fast. The space requirements are linear to the field size for the inversion table and log^2(N) for the multiplication table. This means it is not feasible to use this to generate fields of size 2^32, which would 4*4GB memory.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
g2p::g2p!(GF16, 4, modulus: 0b10011);
let one: GF16 = 1.into();
let a: GF16 = 5.into();
let b: GF16 = 4.into();
let c: GF16 = 7.into();
assert_eq!(a + c, 2.into());
assert_eq!(a - c, 2.into());
assert_eq!(a * b, c);
assert_eq!(a / c, one / b);
assert_eq!(b / b, one);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementation-details)Implementation details

`g2p` generates a new type that implements all the common arithmetic operations. The
calculations are performed on either u8, u16 or u32, depending on the field size.

Addition and subtraction are implemented using regular `Xor`. For division, the divisor inverted
using a precomputed inversion table, which is then multiplied using the multiplication outlined
below

[§](https://docs.rs#multiplication)Multiplication

Multiplication uses a number of precomputed tables to determine the result. Because a full table would grow with the square of the field size, this approach was not deemed feasible. For example, using a full table for GF65536 = GF(2^16), one would need 2^32 entries, which would mean the program reserves 2*4GB just for these tables alone.

Instead a number `n` is split into 8bit components `n = a + 256 * b + 65536 * c ...`. Using this
representation we can multiply two numbers by cross-multiplying all the components
and then adding them up again. So assuming 16bit numbers `n = n0 + 256 * n1` and
`m = m0 + 256 * m1` we get `n*m = n0*m0 + 256*n0*m1 + 256*n1*m0 + 65536*n1*m1`.

We can now create precomputed tables for multiplying the different components together. There is a table for first component times first component, first times second etc. The results then just have to be added together using the normal finite field addition. For our GF65536 example this means the multiplication tables use 4 * 256 * 256 entries á 2 byte which is ~0.5MB

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [g2p](https://docs.rs/macro.g2p.html)
- Procedural macro to generate binary galois fields Generate a newtype of the given name and implement finite field arithmetic on it.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [G2Poly](https://docs.rs/struct.G2Poly.html)
- Polynomial representation of values Main type exported by this library

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Galois](https://docs.rs/trait.GaloisField.html)- Field
- Common trait for finite fields

# lru - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lru/^0.16/

## Expand description

An implementation of a LRU cache. The cache supports `get`, `get_mut`, `put`,
and `pop` operations, all of which are O(1). This crate was heavily influenced
by the [LRU Cache implementation in an earlier version of Rust’s std::collections crate](https://doc.rust-lang.org/0.12.0/std/collections/lru_cache/struct.LruCache.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
extern crate lru;
use lru::LruCache;
use std::num::NonZeroUsize;
fn main() {
        let mut cache = LruCache::new(NonZeroUsize::new(2).unwrap());
        cache.put("apple", 3);
        cache.put("banana", 2);
        assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"apple").unwrap(), 3);
        assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"banana").unwrap(), 2);
        assert!(cache.get(&"pear").is_none());
        assert_eq!(cache.put("banana", 4), Some(2));
        assert_eq!(cache.put("pear", 5), None);
        assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"pear").unwrap(), 5);
        assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"banana").unwrap(), 4);
        assert!(cache.get(&"apple").is_none());
        {
            let v = cache.get_mut(&"banana").unwrap();
            *v = 6;
        }
        assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"banana").unwrap(), 6);
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Into](https://docs.rs/struct.IntoIter.html)- Iter
- An iterator that moves out of a `LruCache`.
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- An iterator over the entries of a `LruCache`.
- [IterMut](https://docs.rs/struct.IterMut.html)
- An iterator over mutables entries of a `LruCache`.
- [LruCache](https://docs.rs/struct.LruCache.html)
- An LRU Cache

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# ferrocat - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ferrocat/2.1.0/ferrocat/

## Expand description

Public Rust entry point for the `ferrocat` workspace.

This crate re-exports the primary API surface from the lower-level
`ferrocat-po` and `ferrocat-icu` crates so application code can depend on a
single package.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

The default feature set is `full`, which enables the complete current API
surface through `catalog` and `serde`.

- `catalog`exposes high-level catalog parsing, updates, combining, audits, machine-translation metadata, plural handling, FCL storage, and runtime artifact compilation.
- `serde`enables serde support in the re-exported- `ferrocat-po`and- `ferrocat-icu`types.
- `compile`,- `mt`, and- `plurals`are reserved subsystem aliases. Today they imply- `catalog`; they do not reduce or split the catalog API surface.

Use `default-features = false` for low-level PO and ICU parsing without the
catalog layer. Enabling `compile`, `mt`, or `plurals` currently has the same
dependency effect as enabling `catalog`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use ferrocat::{icu, po};
let po = po::parse_po("msgid \"Hello\"\nmsgstr \"Hallo\"\n")?;
let icu = icu::parse_icu("Hello {name}")?;
assert_eq!(po.items[0].msgid, "Hello");
assert_eq!(icu.nodes.len(), 2);
```
```
use ferrocat::catalog::{
    CompileSelectedCatalogArtifactOptions, CompiledCatalogIdIndex, CompiledKeyStrategy,
    ParseCatalogOptions, compile_catalog_artifact_selected, parse_catalog,
};
let source = parse_catalog(
    ParseCatalogOptions::new("msgid \"Hello\"\nmsgstr \"Hello\"\n", "en").with_locale("en"),
)?
.into_normalized_view()?;
let requested = parse_catalog(
    ParseCatalogOptions::new("msgid \"Hello\"\nmsgstr \"Hallo\"\n", "en").with_locale("de"),
)?
.into_normalized_view()?;
let index = CompiledCatalogIdIndex::new(&[&requested, &source], CompiledKeyStrategy::FerrocatV1)?;
let compiled_ids = index.iter().map(|(id, _)| id).collect::<Vec<_>>();
let compiled = compile_catalog_artifact_selected(
    &[&requested, &source],
    &index,
    &CompileSelectedCatalogArtifactOptions::new("de", "en", &compiled_ids),
)?;
assert_eq!(compiled.messages.len(), 1);
```
```
use ferrocat::catalog::{
    CatalogAuditOptions, ParseCatalogOptions, audit_catalogs, parse_catalog,
};
let source = parse_catalog(
    ParseCatalogOptions::new("msgid \"Checkout\"\nmsgstr \"Checkout\"\n", "en").with_locale("en"),
)?
.into_normalized_view()?;
let target = parse_catalog(ParseCatalogOptions::new("", "en").with_locale("de"))?
.into_normalized_view()?;
let report = audit_catalogs(&[&source, &target], &CatalogAuditOptions::new("en"))?;
assert!(report.has_errors());
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [catalog](https://docs.rs/catalog/index.html)- `catalog`
- High-level catalog maintenance, audit, and runtime artifact APIs.
- [icu](https://docs.rs/icu/index.html)
- ICU MessageFormat parsing, analysis, compatibility, and metadata APIs.
- [po](https://docs.rs/po/index.html)
- Low-level PO parsing, serialization, and text merge APIs.

- [unescape_](https://docs.rs/fn.unescape_string.html)- string
- Unescapes a PO string literal payload.
- [update_](https://docs.rs/fn.update_catalog.html)- catalog - `catalog`
- Merges extracted messages into an existing catalog and returns updated catalog content.
- [update_](https://docs.rs/fn.update_catalog_file.html)- catalog_ - file - `catalog`
- Updates a catalog on disk and only writes the file when the rendered output changes.
- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_icu.html)- icu
- Validates ICU `MessageFormat`input without returning the parsed AST.
- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_icu_formatter_support.html)- icu_ - formatter_ - support
- Validates ICU formatter usage against a consumer-provided support policy.
- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_icu_formatter_support_from_analysis.html)- icu_ - formatter_ - support_ - from_ - analysis
- Validates analyzed ICU formatter usage against a consumer support policy.
- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_message_metadata.html)- message_ - metadata
- Validates progressive semantic message metadata against its `msgid`.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [IcuFormatter](https://docs.rs/type.IcuFormatterSupportPolicy.html)- Support - Policy - `catalog`
- Callback used to validate runtime support for ICU formatters.

# zeros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/zeros/20.0.0/zeros/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#zeros)Zeros

[§](https://docs.rs#project)Project

- License: GNU Lesser General Public License, either version 3, or (at your option) any later version.
- *This project follows*- [Semantic Versioning 2.0.0](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

This project provides:

- *Some*- [hash functions](https://docs.rs/keccak/index.html)from- [Keccak](https://keccak.team).
- Some cryptographic implementations: [Chacha](https://docs.rs/chacha/index.html),[Poly1305](https://docs.rs/poly1305/index.html),[Argon2](https://docs.rs/argon2/index.html)…

[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

- Currently only little-endian systems are supported. We don’t have access or knowledge to test on big-endian systems.
- Internal state stores data on `u64``u64`natively.
- Accuracy/correctness is highest priority. Speed is second. Currently, it’s slower than well-known implementations, such as
[OpenSSL](https://www.openssl.org).
- Documentation is built with all features. Some of them are optional. If you see components from other crates, you can view source to see what features are required.
- Night Rust is required to build.

[§](https://docs.rs#async-support-understanding-your-responsibilities)Async Support: Understanding Your Responsibilities

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

This crate provides optional async support for cryptographic operations via the `tokio` feature flag. When enabled, it offers
`AsyncRead`/`AsyncWrite` implementations that integrate with the [ tokio](https://docs.rs/tokio) async runtime.

[§](https://docs.rs#important-performance-and-runtime-considerations)Important: Performance and Runtime Considerations

**Cryptographic operations are CPU-bound tasks.** Unlike I/O operations that naturally yield control during waiting periods, cryptographic
functions perform continuous computation without internal await points.

When using this crate’s async API, **you are responsible for managing the balance between computational work and runtime responsiveness.**

[§](https://docs.rs#why-this-matters)Why This Matters

Async runtimes use cooperative scheduling. Tasks are expected to yield control periodically to allow other tasks to make progress. If a single task runs a CPU-intensive operation for too long without yielding, it can:

- Starve other tasks waiting to run
- Delay I/O event processing
- Create noticeable latency spikes
- Potentially deadlock the runtime in extreme cases

[§](https://docs.rs#the-chunk-size-principle)The Chunk Size Principle

The core guideline is: **ensure each chunk of data processed in a single operation is small enough that the cryptographic work completes
within a reasonable time frame for your runtime.**

For example, when calling `write_all()` or `read_exact()` on async streams from this crate:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// ❌ Potentially problematic: Processing 1GB in one call
async_writer.write_all(&huge_data[..]).await?;
// ✅ Better: Process in manageable chunks
for chunk in huge_data.chunks(8 * 1024) {
    async_writer.write_all(chunk).await?;
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#general-guidance)General Guidance

While specific time limits depend on your runtime and hardware, consider these principles:

[§](https://docs.rs#1--runtime-budgets)1.  Runtime budgets

Most async runtimes expect tasks to yield every few hundred microseconds of CPU time. If your chunks are large enough that cryptographic processing exceeds this, you risk starvation.

[§](https://docs.rs#2--test-with-your-workload)2.  **Test with your workload**

The appropriate chunk size depends on:

- Your CPU speed
- The specific cryptographic operation (SHA-3 is slower than Poly1305-ChaCha20)
- Your runtime’s scheduler behavior
- Your application’s latency requirements

[§](https://docs.rs#3--when-in-doubt-use-smaller-chunks)3.  **When in doubt, use smaller chunks**

Processing in smaller chunks (e.g., 8-64 KB) is almost always safer than processing large blocks.

[§](https://docs.rs#alternative-using-blocking-threads)Alternative: Using Blocking Threads

If you need to process large amounts of data and cannot or don’t want to manage chunk sizes, consider using the synchronous API on a blocking thread:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Using tokio as an example, but similar patterns exist for other runtimes
tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || {
    // Use the standard Read/Write API here
    hasher.write_all(&large_data)?;
    let result = hasher.finish();
    // ...
}).await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#what-this-crate-does-not-guarantee)What This Crate Does Not Guarantee

The async API provided by this crate is designed to:

- Follow the `AsyncRead`/`AsyncWrite`contract
- Be compatible with async runtime event loops
- Process data correctly regardless of chunk size

However, it does **not** and **cannot** guarantee:

- That your operation will run within any specific time limit
- That the runtime will remain responsive regardless of how you use it
- Automatic chunking or yield insertion

**These are your responsibility as the user.**

[§](https://docs.rs#understanding-the-trade-off)Understanding the Trade-off

When you enable the `tokio` feature and use this crate’s async API, you are choosing a programming style (async/await) over manual thread
management. This choice gives you better ergonomics and scalability – but with the trade-off that you must be mindful of how long your
tasks run.

This is similar to writing any CPU-intensive operation in an async context: the runtime provides the tools, but you provide the discipline.

[§](https://docs.rs#summary)Summary

[§](https://docs.rs#-do)✅ Do:

- Process data in reasonably sized chunks
- Test your application’s performance under load
- Use blocking threads for truly large operations
- Monitor task latency in production

[§](https://docs.rs#-avoid)❌ Avoid:

- Processing extremely large buffers in single async operations
- Assuming that “async” makes CPU work free
- Ignoring runtime responsiveness in your performance testing

*Remember: The async support in this crate is about programming style and API compatibility. The responsibility for runtime behavior lies
with you, the user.*

# ferrocat_po - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ferrocat-po/2.1.0/ferrocat_po/

## Expand description

Performance-first PO parsing and serialization.

The crate exposes both owned and borrowed parsers for gettext PO files, a byte-oriented UTF-8 parser entry point, plus helpers for serialization and higher-level catalog update workflows.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

The default feature set is `full`, which currently enables the `catalog`
workflow layer.

- `catalog`exposes high-level catalog parsing, updates, combining, audits, machine-translation metadata, plural handling, FCL storage, and runtime artifact compilation. It also enables the catalog-layer dependencies used for hashing, atomic file updates, serde JSON output, ICU diagnostics, and CLDR plural data.
- `serde`enables serde implementations for low-level PO document types and is also enabled by- `catalog`for catalog-layer JSON/report shapes.
- `compile`,- `mt`, and- `plurals`are reserved subsystem aliases. Today they imply- `catalog`; they do not reduce or split the catalog API surface.

Use `default-features = false` for the low-level PO parser, borrowed parser,
serializer, string helpers, and lightweight `merge_catalog` helper without
catalog-layer dependencies. Enabling `compile`, `mt`, or `plurals` currently
has the same dependency effect as enabling `catalog`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use ferrocat_po::{PoFile, SerializeOptions, parse_po, stringify_po};
let input = "msgid \"Hello\"\nmsgstr \"Hallo\"\n";
let file = parse_po(input)?;
assert_eq!(file.items[0].msgid, "Hello");
let output = stringify_po(&file, &SerializeOptions::default());
assert!(output.contains("msgid \"Hello\""));
```
```
use ferrocat_po::parse_po_bytes;
let input = b"msgid \"Hello\"\nmsgstr \"Hallo\"\n";
let file = parse_po_bytes(input)?;
assert_eq!(file.items[0].msgstr[0], "Hallo");
```
```
use ferrocat_po::{
    CompileCatalogArtifactOptions, CompileSelectedCatalogArtifactOptions,
    CompiledCatalogIdIndex, ParseCatalogOptions, compile_catalog_artifact_selected,
    parse_catalog,
};
let source = parse_catalog(
    ParseCatalogOptions::new("msgid \"Hello\"\nmsgstr \"Hello\"\n", "en").with_locale("en"),
)?
.into_normalized_view()?;
let requested = parse_catalog(
    ParseCatalogOptions::new("msgid \"Hello\"\nmsgstr \"Hallo\"\n", "en").with_locale("de"),
)?
.into_normalized_view()?;
let index = CompiledCatalogIdIndex::new(&[&requested, &source], ferrocat_po::CompiledKeyStrategy::FerrocatV1)?;
let compiled_ids = index.iter().map(|(id, _)| id).collect::<Vec<_>>();
let compiled = compile_catalog_artifact_selected(
    &[&requested, &source],
    &index,
    &CompileSelectedCatalogArtifactOptions::new("de", "en", &compiled_ids),
)?;
assert_eq!(compiled.messages.len(), 1);
```
```
use ferrocat_po::{CatalogAuditOptions, ParseCatalogOptions, audit_catalogs, parse_catalog};
let source = parse_catalog(
    ParseCatalogOptions::new("msgid \"Hello {name}\"\nmsgstr \"Hello {name}\"\n", "en")
        .with_locale("en"),
)?
.into_normalized_view()?;
let target = parse_catalog(
    ParseCatalogOptions::new("msgid \"Hello {name}\"\nmsgstr \"Hallo\"\n", "en")
        .with_locale("de"),
)?
.into_normalized_view()?;
let report = audit_catalogs(&[&source, &target], &CatalogAuditOptions::new("en"))?;
assert!(report.has_errors());
```

# shikumi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/shikumi/0.1.129/shikumi/

## Expand description

Shikumi (仕組み) — config discovery, hot-reload, and `ArcSwap` store
for Nix-managed desktop applications.

Extracted from [karakuri](https://github.com/pleme-io/karakuri)’s configuration
system, shikumi provides the shared infrastructure for desktop apps that need:

- **XDG config discovery**with env var overrides and format preference
- **Figment provider chains**(defaults → env vars → config file)
- **Lock-free concurrent reads**via- `ArcSwap`
- **Hot-reload**with symlink-aware file watching (for nix-darwin managed configs)

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use serde::Deserialize;
use shikumi::{ConfigDiscovery, ConfigStore, Format};
#[derive(Deserialize, Clone, Debug, Default)]
struct MyConfig {
    window_width: Option<u32>,
}
let path = ConfigDiscovery::new("myapp")
    .env_override("MYAPP_CONFIG")
    .formats(&[Format::Yaml, Format::Toml])
    .discover()
    .expect("config file not found");
let store = ConfigStore::<MyConfig>::load(&path, "MYAPP_")
    .expect("failed to load config");
let config = store.get();
println!("width: {:?}", config.window_width);
```

- [tiered_](https://docs.rs/macro.tiered_permutation_test.html)- permutation_ - test
- Emit ONE matrix `#[test]`that stamps every cube cell onto every config tier, serde-round-trips each, runs a user`apply`closure, and aggregates EVERY failure before asserting.

- Closed discipline trait for the `ProductCube``invert(cell) = Some(image)`exactly on the realizable cells,`None`on the cross-axis consistency-violation complement.
- [Product](https://docs.rs/trait.ProductCube.html)- Cube
- Closed discipline trait every typescape product cube satisfies — a
refinement of `ClosedAxis`

# ferrocat_icu - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ferrocat-icu/2.1.0/ferrocat_icu/

## Expand description

Compact, performance-oriented ICU `MessageFormat` parsing primitives.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use ferrocat_icu::{extract_variables, parse_icu};
let message = parse_icu("Hello {name}, you have {count, plural, one {# item} other {# items}}.")?;
assert_eq!(extract_variables(&message), vec!["name", "count"]);
```
```
use ferrocat_icu::{
    IcuCompatibilityOptions, analyze_icu, compare_icu_messages, parse_icu,
};
let source = parse_icu("Hello {name}, you have {count, number, integer} files.")?;
let translation = parse_icu("Hallo, du hast {count, number, integer} Dateien.")?;
let source_analysis = analyze_icu(&source);
assert_eq!(source_analysis.arguments.len(), 2);
let report = compare_icu_messages(
    &source,
    &translation,
    &IcuCompatibilityOptions::default(),
);
assert!(report.has_errors());
```
```
use ferrocat_icu::{
    MessageArgumentKind, MessageMetadataInput, normalize_message_metadata,
};
let metadata = normalize_message_metadata(MessageMetadataInput::new(
    "{count, plural, one {One item} other {# items}}",
))?;
assert_eq!(
    metadata.args.get("count").map(|argument| argument.kind),
    Some(MessageArgumentKind::Number)
);
assert!(metadata.selectors.contains_key("count"));
```
```
use ferrocat_icu::{parse_icu, stringify_icu};
let parsed = parse_icu("Hello {name}")?;
assert_eq!(stringify_icu(&parsed), "Hello {name}");
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [diagnostic_](https://docs.rs/diagnostic_codes/index.html)- codes
- Stable machine-readable diagnostic codes emitted by `ferrocat-icu`.

# everruns_gemini - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-gemini/0.17.3/everruns_gemini/

## Expand description

Google Gemini LLM provider driver for Everruns.

`everruns-gemini` is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com) ecosystem.
It implements the `ChatDriver` contract from `everruns-core`, so the agent
loop can run against Google’s Gemini API, and registers itself through
[ register_driver](https://docs.rs/fn.register_driver.html).

Core has no knowledge of specific providers; hosts register whichever drivers
they want available via `register_driver` at startup.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_gemini::register_driver;
use everruns_core::DriverRegistry;
let mut registry = DriverRegistry::new();
register_driver(&mut registry);
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Driver](https://docs.rs/struct.DriverRegistry.html)- Registry
- Registry for LLM drivers
- [Gemini](https://docs.rs/struct.GeminiChatDriver.html)- Chat - Driver
- Google Gemini Chat Driver

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Chat](https://docs.rs/trait.ChatDriver.html)- Driver
- Trait for LLM drivers

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [register_](https://docs.rs/fn.register_driver.html)- driver
- Register the Gemini driver with the driver registry

# everruns_bedrock - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-bedrock/0.17.3/everruns_bedrock/

## Expand description

AWS Bedrock Runtime provider driver for Everruns.

`everruns-bedrock` implements the [ ChatDriver](https://docs.rs/trait.ChatDriver.html) contract from

`everruns-core`
using the AWS Bedrock Runtime `ConverseStream` API.Credentials are encoded as JSON in the `api_key` field:

`{"access_key_id":"...","secret_access_key":"...","session_token":"...","region":"us-east-1"}``session_token` is optional. The `base_url` field is unused.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_bedrock::{BedrockChatDriver, register_driver};
use everruns_core::DriverRegistry;
let mut registry = DriverRegistry::new();
register_driver(&mut registry);
```

- [Bedrock](https://docs.rs/struct.BedrockChatDriver.html)- Chat - Driver
- AWS Bedrock Runtime Chat Driver.
- [Driver](https://docs.rs/struct.DriverRegistry.html)- Registry
- Registry for LLM drivers

- [Chat](https://docs.rs/trait.ChatDriver.html)- Driver
- Trait for LLM drivers

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [register_](https://docs.rs/fn.register_driver.html)- driver
- Register the Bedrock driver with the given registry.

# azalea_reflection_proxy - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/azalea-reflection-proxy/0.1.1/azalea_reflection_proxy/

## Expand description

azalea-reflection-proxy — spectate and control an azalea bot session through a local reflection proxy. Rust port of aesthetic0001/mineflayer-reflection-proxy.

The proxy owns the single real (Microsoft-authed) connection to the
target server. Your bot connects to the proxy locally as an offline
client and becomes the controller; vanilla clients that join the
same local address become spectators, see the bot as a live player
entity, and can take over with `,acquire`.

```
use azalea_reflection_proxy::ReflectionProxy;
let proxy = ReflectionProxy::builder()
    .target("mc.hypixel.net")
    .email("you@example.com")
    .spawn()
    .await?;
// then point your azalea bot at it instead of the real server:
//   ClientBuilder::new()
//       .set_handler(handle)
//       .start(Account::offline("reflected"), proxy.local_addr())
// and add a vanilla-client server entry for the same address to
// spectate. proxy.local_addr() is a real SocketAddr, so a bound
// port of 0 picks a free one.
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use plugin::`- [Frame](https://docs.rs/plugin/struct.Frame.html);
- `pub use plugin::`- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/plugin/struct.Pipeline.html);
- `pub use plugin::`- [ProxyPlugin](https://docs.rs/plugin/trait.ProxyPlugin.html);
- `pub use plugin::`- [Verdict](https://docs.rs/plugin/enum.Verdict.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [plugin](https://docs.rs/plugin/index.html)
- Plugin pipeline — the azalea equivalent of the JS project’s plugin system (anonymize / snapshot / synchronization / inventory / replicator).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Proxy](https://docs.rs/struct.ProxyBuilder.html)- Builder
- Configuration for a reflection proxy. Build with
`ReflectionProxy::builder`
- [Reflection](https://docs.rs/struct.ReflectionProxy.html)- Proxy
- A running reflection proxy. Dropping the handle does NOT stop it;
call `Self::shutdown`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Proxy](https://docs.rs/enum.ProxyEvent.html)- Event
- Things happening inside the proxy that the host program may care
about — the port of the original’s `clientJoin`/`changeControl`server events. Subscribe with`ReflectionProxy::subscribe`

# everruns_openrouter - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-openrouter/0.17.3/everruns_openrouter/

## Expand description

OpenRouter provider driver for Everruns.

`everruns-openrouter` is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com)
ecosystem. It implements the [ ChatDriver](https://docs.rs/trait.ChatDriver.html) contract from

`everruns-core`
and registers the OpenRouter provider into a [.](https://docs.rs/struct.DriverRegistry.html)

`DriverRegistry`OpenRouter exposes an OpenAI-compatible Responses API, so [ OpenRouterChatDriver](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenRouterChatDriver.html)
wraps

`everruns_core::OpenResponsesProtocolChatDriver` tagged with
`DriverId::OpenRouter`. Its `/models` endpoint advertises richer metadata
(a `supported_parameters` array) that the crate parses into capability
profiles at discovery time.[§](https://docs.rs#registering-the-driver)Registering the Driver

```
use everruns_core::DriverRegistry;
use everruns_openrouter::register_driver;
let mut registry = DriverRegistry::new();
register_driver(&mut registry);
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Driver](https://docs.rs/struct.DriverRegistry.html)- Registry
- Registry for LLM drivers
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenRouterArchitecture.html)- Router - Architecture
- Modality metadata from OpenRouter’s `architecture`object.
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenRouterChatDriver.html)- Router - Chat - Driver
- OpenRouter driver using its OpenAI-compatible Responses API.
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenRouterModelInfo.html)- Router - Model - Info
- Individual model entry from OpenRouter’s models API.
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenRouterModelsResponse.html)- Router - Models - Response
- Response from OpenRouter’s `/api/v1/models`endpoint.
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenRouterPricing.html)- Router - Pricing
- Per-token pricing reported by OpenRouter’s `pricing`object.
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenRouterRequestExtension.html)- Router - Request - Extension
- Layers OpenRouter-specific fields onto an Open Responses request body.
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenRouterTopProvider.html)- Router - TopProvider
- Per-request limits reported by the routed upstream provider.

- [Chat](https://docs.rs/trait.ChatDriver.html)- Driver
- Trait for LLM drivers

- Register the OpenRouter driver with the driver registry.

# sim_lib_music_lower - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-music-lower/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_music_lower/

## Expand description

Lowers music from higher-level representations to renderable ones.

Lowering is the inverse of lifting: it takes a structured music object or
[ Score](https://docs.rs/sim-lib-music-core/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_lib_music_core/model/struct.Score.html) and renders it down to a concrete,
playable Standard MIDI File.

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.lower.html)

`lower`[produce an in-memory](https://docs.rs/fn.lower_score.html)

`lower_score``SmfFile`, while [serializes that file to bytes.](https://docs.rs/fn.write_smf.html)

`write_smf`[controls ticks-per-quarter resolution, the tempo map, and how voices are split across MIDI tracks.](https://docs.rs/struct.LowerOpts.html)

`LowerOpts`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Lower](https://docs.rs/struct.LowerOpts.html)- Opts
- Options controlling how music is lowered to a MIDI file.
- [Tempo](https://docs.rs/struct.TempoMap.html)- Map
- A piecewise-constant tempo curve mapping music time to beats per minute.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Lower](https://docs.rs/enum.LowerError.html)- Error
- Error raised while lowering music to a MIDI file.
- [Track](https://docs.rs/enum.TrackSplit.html)- Split
- Policy for distributing lowered notes across MIDI tracks.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_us_per_quarter.html)- us_ - per_ - quarter
- Returns the default microseconds-per-quarter-note tempo value.
- [equivalent_](https://docs.rs/fn.equivalent_under_lowering.html)- under_ - lowering
- Returns whether two music objects lower to byte-identical MIDI files.
- [lower](https://docs.rs/fn.lower.html)
- Lowers any music object into an in-memory MIDI file.
- [lower_](https://docs.rs/fn.lower_score.html)- score
- Lowers a `Score`into a MIDI file, applying the score’s tempo to the map.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_smf.html)- smf
- Lowers a `Score`and serializes the resulting MIDI file to bytes.

# everruns_anthropic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-anthropic/0.17.3/everruns_anthropic/

## Expand description

Anthropic Claude provider driver for Everruns.

`everruns-anthropic` is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com)
ecosystem. It implements the [ ChatDriver](https://docs.rs/trait.ChatDriver.html) contract from

`everruns-core` and
registers Anthropic’s Messages API driver into a [.](https://docs.rs/struct.DriverRegistry.html)

`DriverRegistry`Provider crates depend on `everruns-core`; `everruns-core` does not depend on
provider implementations. Hosts register whichever drivers they want to make
available.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_anthropic::{AnthropicChatDriver, register_driver};
use everruns_core::DriverRegistry;
let driver = AnthropicChatDriver::new("your-api-key");
let mut registry = DriverRegistry::new();
register_driver(&mut registry);
assert!(format!("{driver:?}").contains("AnthropicChatDriver"));
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Anthropic](https://docs.rs/struct.AnthropicChatDriver.html)- Chat - Driver
- Anthropic Claude Chat Driver
- [Driver](https://docs.rs/struct.DriverRegistry.html)- Registry
- Registry for LLM drivers

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Chat](https://docs.rs/trait.ChatDriver.html)- Driver
- Trait for LLM drivers

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [register_](https://docs.rs/fn.register_driver.html)- driver
- Register the Anthropic driver with the driver registry

# rtotp 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rtotp/0.1.0

rtotp-0.1.0 is not a library.

                # rtotp

Rust one-Time Password - a small terminal TOTP (RFC 6238) client.

## Demo

## Install

Download a prebuilt binary from the [releases page](https://github.com/goodhee/rtotp/releases),
or build from source:

```
# or, from a checkout:
```
## Usage

```
rtotp <command>
  <n>       Show the current 6-digit code for entry n (see `list`)
  add       Add a new OTP secret (Issuer, Account Name, Secret)
  list      List registered secrets
  remove    Remove an entry (prompts if index omitted)
  clear     Remove all entries
```
Example:

`rtotp 1` is shorthand for `rtotp code 1`.

## Notes

- The secret is stored locally in plaintext at `~/.rtotplist`(file mode`0600`). Treat the machine as the trust boundary.
- Codes are standard TOTP: SHA1, 6 digits, 30s period - compatible with most authenticators and OTP-issuing apps.

## License

MIT

# rqrr 0.10.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rqrr/0.10.1

# rust-qr-reader - Find and read QR-Codes

This crates exports functions and types that can be used to search for QR-Codes in images and decode them.

## Usage

The most basic usage is shown below:

```
use image;
use rqrr;
let img = open?.to_luma;
// Prepare for detection
let mut img = prepare;
// Search for grids, without decoding
let grids = img.detect_grids;
assert_eq!;
// Decode the grid
let  = grids.decode?;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
For more information visit [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/rqrr/)

## License

## Attribution

This library was made on the base of [quirc](https://github.com/dlbeer/quirc)

# rqrr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rqrr/0.10.1/target-redirect/rqrr/

## Expand description

Find and read QR-Codes

This crates exports functions and types that can be used to search for QR-Codes in images and decode them.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The most basic usage is shown below:

```
use image;
// Load on image to search, convert it to grayscale
let img = image::open("tests/data/github.gif")?.to_luma8();
// Prepare for detection
let mut img = rqrr::PreparedImage::prepare(img);
// Search for grids, without decoding
let grids = img.detect_grids();
assert_eq!(grids.len(), 1);
// Decode the grid
let (meta, content) = grids[0].decode()?;
assert_eq!(meta.ecc_level, 0);
assert_eq!(content, "https://github.com/WanzenBug/rqrr");
```
If you have some other form of picture storage, you can use
[ PreparedImage::prepare_from_*](https://docs.rs/struct.PreparedImage.html). This allows
you to define your own source for images.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Grid](https://docs.rs/struct.Grid.html)
- Wrapper around any grid that can be interpreted as a QR code
- [Meta](https://docs.rs/struct.MetaData.html)- Data
- MetaData for a QR grid
- [Mirrored](https://docs.rs/struct.MirroredGrid.html)- Grid
- Mirrored grid, switching x and y coordinates
- [Point](https://docs.rs/struct.Point.html)
- A simple point in (some) space
- [Prepared](https://docs.rs/struct.PreparedImage.html)- Image
- An black-and-white image that can be mutated on search for QR codes
- [RawData](https://docs.rs/struct.RawData.html)
- The bit stream contained in the QR Code
- [Simple](https://docs.rs/struct.SimpleGrid.html)- Grid
- A basic GridImage that can be generated from a given function.
- [Version](https://docs.rs/struct.Version.html)
- Version of a QR Code which determines its size

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [DeQR](https://docs.rs/enum.DeQRError.html)- Error
- Possible errors that can happen during decoding

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [BitGrid](https://docs.rs/trait.BitGrid.html)
- A grid that contains exactly one QR code square.

---

[141](#141)        let mut dyn_img = image::GrayImage::new(self.size() as u32, self.size() as u32);

[255](#255)}
[256](#256)
[257](#257)impl SimpleGrid {
[258](#258)    pub fn from_func<F>(size: usize, fill_func: F) -> Self
[259](#259)    where
[260](#260)        F: Fn(usize, usize) -> bool,
[261](#261)    {
[262](#262)        let mut cell_bitmap = vec![0; (size * size + 7) / 8];
[263](#263)        let mut c = 0;
[264](#264)        for y in 0..size {
[265](#265)            for x in 0..size {
[266](#266)                if fill_func(x, y) {
[267](#267)                    cell_bitmap[c >> 3] |= 1 << (c & 7) as u8;
[268](#268)                }
[269](#269)                c += 1;
[270](#270)            }
[271](#271)        }
[272](#272)
[273](#273)        SimpleGrid { cell_bitmap, size }
[274](#274)    }

[282](#282)    fn bit(&self, y: usize, x: usize) -> bool {
[283](#283)        let c = y * self.size + x;
[284](#284)        self.cell_bitmap[c >> 3] & (1 << (c & 7) as u8) != 0
[285](#285)    }

[321](#321)impl ::std::fmt::Display for DeQRError {
[322](#322)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
[323](#323)        let msg = match self {
[324](#324)            DeQRError::IoError => "IoError(Could not write to output)",
[325](#325)            DeQRError::DataUnderflow => "DataUnderflow(Expected more bits to decode)",
[326](#326)            DeQRError::DataOverflow => "DataOverflow(Expected less bits to decode)",
[327](#327)            DeQRError::UnknownDataType => "UnknownDataType(DataType not known or not implemented)",
[328](#328)            DeQRError::DataEcc => "Ecc(Too many errors to correct)",
[329](#329)            DeQRError::FormatEcc => "Ecc(Version information corrupt)",
[330](#330)            DeQRError::InvalidVersion => "InvalidVersion(Invalid version or corrupt)",
[331](#331)            DeQRError::InvalidGridSize => "InvalidGridSize(Invalid version or corrupt)",
[332](#332)            DeQRError::EncodingError => "Encoding(Not UTF8)",
[333](#333)        };
[334](#334)        write!(f, "{msg}")
[335](#335)    }

# PreparedImage in rqrr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rqrr/0.10.1/rqrr/struct.PreparedImage.html

`pub struct PreparedImage<S> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

An black-and-white image that can be mutated on search for QR codes

During search for QR codes, some black zones will be recolored in ‘different’ shades of black. This is done to speed up the search and mitigate the impact of a huge zones.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

    S: ImageBuffer,

# Grid in rqrr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rqrr/0.10.1/rqrr/struct.Grid.html

# Struct Grid

[Source](../src/rqrr/lib.rs.html#54-65) ```
pub struct Grid<G> {
    pub grid: G,
    pub bounds: [
```
[Point](struct.Point.html); [4](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html)],
}

## Expand description

Wrapper around any grid that can be interpreted as a QR code

The backing binary square

The bounds of the square, in underlying coordinates.

The points are listed in the following order:
[top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left]

If this grid references for example an underlying image, these values
will be set to coordinates in that image.

Create a new grid from a BitGrid.

This just initialises the bounds to 0.

Try to decode the grid.

If successful returns the decoded string as well as metadata about the
code.

Try to read metadata, and return the raw, uncorrected bit stream.

If successful, returns the metadata along with the raw bit pattern.
The raw data is still masked, so bits appear as in the source image.

Try to decode the grid.

Instead of returning a String, this method writes the decoded result to
the given writer

**Warning**: This may lead to half decoded content to be written to the
writer.

Performs copy-assignment from

`source`.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html#method.clone_from)

Formats the value using the given formatter.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html#tymethod.fmt)

Immutably borrows from an owned value.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html#tymethod.borrow)

Mutably borrows from an owned value.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.BorrowMut.html#tymethod.borrow_mut)

🔬This is a nightly-only experimental API. (`clone_to_uninit`)

Performs copy-assignment from

`self` to

`dest`.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.CloneToUninit.html#tymethod.clone_to_uninit)

Returns the argument unchanged.

Calls `U::from(self)`.

That is, this conversion is whatever the implementation of
[From](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)<T> for U

The resulting type after obtaining ownership.

Creates owned data from borrowed data, usually by cloning.

# MirroredGrid in rqrr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rqrr/0.10.1/rqrr/struct.MirroredGrid.html

`pub struct MirroredGrid<'a>(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

Mirrored grid, switching x and y coordinates

Some QR codes are read mirrored, even though the spec does not officially support it. Since there is no marker in the QR code spec, we simply have to try to read the grid both ways if the first does not succeed.

# DeQRError in rqrr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rqrr/0.10.1/rqrr/enum.DeQRError.html

```
pub enum DeQRError {
    IoError,
    DataUnderflow,
    DataOverflow,
    UnknownDataType,
    DataEcc,
    FormatEcc,
    InvalidVersion,
    InvalidGridSize,
    EncodingError,
}
```
## Expand description

Possible errors that can happen during decoding

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.IoError)

### IoError

Could not write the output to the output stream/string

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.DataUnderflow)

### DataUnderflow

Expected more bits to decode

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.DataOverflow)

### DataOverflow

Expected less bits to decode

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.UnknownDataType)

### UnknownDataType

Unknown data type in encoding

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.DataEcc)

### DataEcc

Could not correct errors / code corrupt

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.FormatEcc)

### FormatEcc

Could not read format information from both locations

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidVersion)

### InvalidVersion

Unsupported / non-existent version read

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidGridSize)

### InvalidGridSize

Unsupported / non-existent grid size read

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.EncodingError)

### EncodingError

Output was not encoded in expected UTF8

# rqrr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rqrr/latest/rqrr/

## Expand description

Find and read QR-Codes

This crates exports functions and types that can be used to search for QR-Codes in images and decode them.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The most basic usage is shown below:

```
use image;
// Load on image to search, convert it to grayscale
let img = image::open("tests/data/github.gif")?.to_luma8();
// Prepare for detection
let mut img = rqrr::PreparedImage::prepare(img);
// Search for grids, without decoding
let grids = img.detect_grids();
assert_eq!(grids.len(), 1);
// Decode the grid
let (meta, content) = grids[0].decode()?;
assert_eq!(meta.ecc_level, 0);
assert_eq!(content, "https://github.com/WanzenBug/rqrr");
```
If you have some other form of picture storage, you can use
[ PreparedImage::prepare_from_*](https://docs.rs/struct.PreparedImage.html). This allows
you to define your own source for images.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Grid](https://docs.rs/struct.Grid.html)
- Wrapper around any grid that can be interpreted as a QR code
- [Meta](https://docs.rs/struct.MetaData.html)- Data
- MetaData for a QR grid
- [Mirrored](https://docs.rs/struct.MirroredGrid.html)- Grid
- Mirrored grid, switching x and y coordinates
- [Point](https://docs.rs/struct.Point.html)
- A simple point in (some) space
- [Prepared](https://docs.rs/struct.PreparedImage.html)- Image
- An black-and-white image that can be mutated on search for QR codes
- [RawData](https://docs.rs/struct.RawData.html)
- The bit stream contained in the QR Code
- [Simple](https://docs.rs/struct.SimpleGrid.html)- Grid
- A basic GridImage that can be generated from a given function.
- [Version](https://docs.rs/struct.Version.html)
- Version of a QR Code which determines its size

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [DeQR](https://docs.rs/enum.DeQRError.html)- Error
- Possible errors that can happen during decoding

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [BitGrid](https://docs.rs/trait.BitGrid.html)
- A grid that contains exactly one QR code square.

---

# rqrr 0.10.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rqrr/latest/builds

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

# lru 0.16.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lru/^0.16

# LRU Cache

An implementation of a LRU cache. The cache supports `put`, `get`, `get_mut` and `pop` operations,
all of which are O(1). This crate was heavily influenced by the [LRU Cache implementation in an
earlier version of Rust's std::collections crate](https://doc.rust-lang.org/0.12.0/std/collections/lru_cache/struct.LruCache.html).

The MSRV for this crate is 1.70.0.

## Example

Below is a simple example of how to instantiate and use a LRU cache.

```
extern crate lru;
use LruCache;
use NonZeroUsize;
```

# rust-qr-reader - Find and read QR-Codes

assert_eq!;

# rqrr 0.10.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rqrr/latest/source/README.md

```
[![documentation](https://docs.rs/rqrr/badge.svg)](https://docs.rs/rqrr/)
[![Build Status](https://github.com/WanzenBug/rqrr/actions/workflows/CI.yaml/badge.svg?branch=master)](https://github.com/WanzenBug/rqrr/actions/workflows/CI.yaml)
This crates exports functions and types that can be used to search for QR-Codes in images and
decode them.
The most basic usage is shown below:
```rust
use image;
use rqrr;
let img = image::open("tests/data/github.gif")?.to_luma();
// Prepare for detection
let mut img = rqrr::PreparedImage::prepare(img);
// Search for grids, without decoding
let grids = img.detect_grids();
assert_eq!(grids.len(), 1);
// Decode the grid
let (meta, content) = grids[0].decode()?;
assert_eq!(meta.ecc_level, 0);
assert_eq!(content, "https://github.com/WanzenBug/rqrr");
```
For more information visit [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/rqrr/)
Either [APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or [MIT](LICENSE-MIT)
This library was made on the base of [quirc](https://github.com/dlbeer/quirc)
```

# g2p 1.2.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/g2p/1.2.2

# g2p

This crate can generate types that implement fast finite field arithmetic. Many error correcting codes rely on some form of finite field of the form GF(2^p), where p is relatively small. Similarly some cryptographic algorithms such as AES use finite field arithmetic.

While addition and subtraction can be done quickly using just a simple XOR, multiplication is more involved. To speed things up, you can use a precomputed table. Typically this table is just copied into the source code directly. Using this crate, you can have the benefits in speed of precomputed table, without the need to create your own type with custom multiplication and division implementation.

## WARNING

The types generated by this library are probably not suitable for cryptographic purposes, as multiplication is not guaranteed to be constant time.

## Note

The implementation was tested for finite fields up to 217 in size, which compiles reasonably
fast. The space requirements are linear to the field size for the inversion table and log2(N)
for the multiplication table. This means it is not feasible to use this to generate fields of
size 2^32, which would 4*4GB memory.

## Examples

```
use g2p;
g2p::g2p!(GF16, 4, modulus: 0b10011);
let one: GF16 = 1.into();
let a: GF16 = 5.into();
let b: GF16 = 4.into();
let c: GF16 = 7.into();
assert_eq!(a + c, 2.into());
assert_eq!(a - c, 2.into());
assert_eq!(a * b, c);
assert_eq!(a / c, one / b);
assert_eq!(b / b, one);
```
## Performance

There is a benchmark suite comparing the result of this crate to [galois_2p8](https://crates.io/crates/galois_2p8)
and [reed-solomon-erasure](https://crates.io/crates/reed-solomon-erasure) which both implement a finite field with 256
elements.

Note that the competing libraries implement some special functionality to improve performance when one of the operands is fixed. Here are the results:

## Implementation details

`g2p` generates a new type that implements all the common arithmetic operations. The
calculations are performed on either u8, u16 or u32, depending on the field size.

Addition and subtraction are implemented using regular `Xor`. For division, the divisor inverted
using a precomputed inversion table, which is then multiplied using the multiplication outlined
below

### Multiplication

Multiplication uses a number of precomputed tables to determine the result. Because a full table
would grow with the square of the field size, this approach was not deemed feasible. For
example, using a full table for GF65536 = GF(216), one would need 232 entries, which would
mean the program reserves 2*4GB just for these tables alone.

Instead a number `n` is split into 8bit components `n = a + 256 * b + 65536 * c ...`. Using this
representation we can multiply two numbers by cross-multiplying all the components
and then adding them up again. So assuming 16bit numbers `n = n0 + 256 * n1` and
`m = m0 + 256 * m1` we get `n*m = n0*m0 + 256*n0*m1 + 256*n1*m0 + 65536*n1*m1`.

We can now create precomputed tables for multiplying the different components together. There is a table for first component times first component, first times second etc. The results then just have to be added together using the normal finite field addition. For our GF65536 example this means the multiplication tables use 4 * 256 * 256 entries á 2 byte which is ~0.5MB

## License

Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)
or the MIT license [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)>, at your
option.

---

# g2poly - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/g2poly/^1.2/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#g2poly)g2poly

A small library to handle polynomials of degree < 64 over the finite field GF(2).

The main motivation for this library is generating finite fields of the form GF(2^p). Elements of GF(2^p) can be expressed as polynomials over GF(2) with degree < p. These finite fields are used in cryptographic algorithms as well as error detecting / correcting codes.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use g2poly;
let a = g2poly::G2Poly(0b10011);
assert_eq!(format!("{}", a), "G2Poly { x^4 + x + 1 }");
let b = g2poly::G2Poly(0b1);
assert_eq!(a + b, g2poly::G2Poly(0b10010));
// Since products could overflow in u64, the product is defined as a u128
assert_eq!(a * a, g2poly::G2PolyProd(0b100000101));
// This can be reduced using another polynomial
let s = a * a % g2poly::G2Poly(0b1000000);
assert_eq!(s, g2poly::G2Poly(0b101));
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [G2Poly](https://docs.rs/struct.G2Poly.html)
- Main type exported by this library
- [G2Poly](https://docs.rs/struct.G2PolyProd.html)- Prod
- The result of multiplying two `G2Poly`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [extended_](https://docs.rs/fn.extended_gcd.html)- gcd
- Calculate the greatest common divisor with Bézout coefficients
- [gcd](https://docs.rs/fn.gcd.html)
- Calculate the greatest common divisor of `a`and`b`

# criterion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/criterion/^0.4/

## Expand description

A statistics-driven micro-benchmarking library written in Rust.

This crate is a microbenchmarking library which aims to provide strong statistical confidence in detecting and estimating the size of performance improvements and regressions, while also being easy to use.

See
[the user guide](https://bheisler.github.io/criterion.rs/book/index.html)
for examples as well as details on the measurement and analysis process,
and the output.

- Collects detailed statistics, providing strong confidence that changes to performance are real, not measurement noise.
- Produces detailed charts, providing thorough understanding of your code’s performance behavior.

This module defines a trait that can be used to plug in different Futures executors into Criterion.rs’ async benchmarking support.

This module defines a set of traits that can be used to plug different measurements (eg.
Unix’s Processor Time, CPU or GPU performance counters, etc.) into Criterion.rs. It also
includes the [WallTime](https://docs.rs/struct.WallTime.html) struct which defines the default wall-clock time
measurement.

This module provides an extension trait which allows in-process profilers
to be hooked into the `--profile-time` argument at compile-time. Users of
out-of-process profilers such as perf don’t need to do anything special.

Macro used to define a function group for the benchmark harness; see the
`criterion_main!` macro for more details.

Structure used to group together a set of related benchmarks, along with custom configuration settings for groups of benchmarks. All benchmarks performed using a benchmark group will be grouped together in the final report.

Simple structure representing an ID for a benchmark. The ID must be unique within a benchmark group.

This enum allows the user to control how Criterion.rs chooses the iteration count when sampling. The default is Auto, which will choose a method automatically based on the iteration time during the warm-up phase.

Enum representing different ways of measuring the throughput of benchmarked code. If the throughput setting is configured for a benchmark then the estimated throughput will be reported as well as the time per iteration.

# galois_2p8 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/galois_2p8/^0.1.2/

## Expand description

Provides operations over all `GF(2^8)` extensions.

[§](https://docs.rs#fields-1)Fields

Fields are sets of values over which addition, subtraction, multiplication and division are defined, such that the results of these operations are still members of the defined set and the following properties hold:

- Associativity: `a + (b + c) == (a + b) + c`.
- Commutativity: `a + b`==`b + a`and`a * b == b * a`.
- Identity: There exists a `0`and`1`element such that`a + 0 == a`and`a * 1 == a`.
- Additive inverse: For every `a`there is some`-a`such that`a + -a == 0`.
- Multiplicative inverse: For every `a`there is some`a^-1`such that`a * a^-1 == 1`.
- Distributivity: `a * (b + c) == a * b + b * c`.

The set of real numbers constitutes a field, but said set is not the only possible field.

[§](https://docs.rs#galois-fields)Galois Fields

Galois fields are finite fields: a limited number of possible members are
defined. The number of unique members of a Galois field is called the order
of the field. Galois fields only exist for integers that are also powers
of prime numbers. The prime base of an order is called the characteristic
of the field. For any Galois field with a characteristic of `c`, for all
members of the field `m`, `let sum = 0; for i in 0..c { sum += m }; sum == 0`.

Galois fields with non-prime orders are defined in terms of polynomials with
the coefficients being members of the field defined by the characteristic as
the order. This maps directly to the representation of numbers in terms of
their base. The resulting field is considered an *extension* of the field
generated by the characteristic.

For example, a Galois field with an order of 256 necessarily has a
characteristic of 2, because 2 is the least prime base of 256. As a result,
`GF(256) == GF(2^8)` is defined in terms of an order 8 polynomial, taking
the form

`k_8*x^8 + k_7*x^7 + k_6*x^6 + k_5*x^5 + k_4*x^4 + k_3*x^3 + k_2*x^2 + k_1*x + k_0`

where `k_n in [0, 1] for n in [0..8]`.

Similar to non-extension fields being defined over prime numbers, extensions
are defined over prime polynomials, that is, multiplication and division are
performed modulo some polynomial that cannot be represented as the result
of the multiplication of two polynomial factors. These prime polynomials are
known as *irreducable polynomials*, because they cannot be reduced to
factors.

[§](https://docs.rs#primitive-polynomials)Primitive Polynomials

Consider the exponential operation `a ^ b`. In Galois fields, this is still
defined in terms of repeated multiplication of `a` times itself over `b`
iterations. Consider also a Galois field defined over an irreducable
polynomial `p`. If `a` is prime, but also the member of a given field, and
for every member `b` in the field, `a ^ b` corresponds to exactly one other
member of the field, then we say that `p` is a *primitive polynomial*,
because the entirety of the field members can be represented in terms of
exponents and logarithms about the base `a`.

[§](https://docs.rs#gf2x-on-hardware)`GF(2^x)` on Hardware

The definition of finite fields with a characteristic of 2 results in addition and subtraction mapping directly to bitwise XOR. Consider that:

- `0 +/- 0 == 0; 0 XOR 0 == 0`
- `1 +/- 0 == 1; 1 XOR 0 == 1`
- `0 +/- 1 == 1; 0 XOR 1 == 1`
- `1 +/- 1 == 0; 1 XOR 1 == 0`

Multiplication and division are slightly more difficult. Multiplication is still defined as repeated addition of coefficients within the field, but is performed modulo the primitive polynomial, which requires taking the remainder of divison. Division within the field is purely defined as the inverse of multiplication, with no canonical polynomial-time algorithm. (This ostensible incongruity of computational complexity between multiplication and division forms the basis of several areas of study in cryptography).

If the size of the field is small enough, multiplication and division can
be performed by way of table lookups. For non-primitive polynomials, the
size of the lookup tables can be reduced by decomposing operations
according to the field properties. For example, `a * b == (a_1 + a_2) * b == a_1 * b + a_2 * b`, where a_1 represents the upper bits of `a` and `a_2`
represents the lower bits of `a`. As a result, the required storage space
is reduced by a factor of `2 ^ (x - 5)`. For primitive polynomials,
the operations can be performed in terms of exponentials and logarithms,
which only requires two to five times as many entries as members of the
field, depending on the implementation. `galois_2p8` currently uses
tables requiring three times the size of the field for multiplication
and division for primitive polynomials.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-galois_2p8-crate)The `galois_2p8` Crate

This crate implements `GF(2^8)` arithmetic for all possible irreducable
polynomials. The possible irreducable polynomials are represented as members
of the [ IrreducablePolynomial](https://docs.rs/field/enum.IrreducablePolynomial.html) enumeration. Each

[is passed as an argument to the constructor of a struct implementing the](https://docs.rs/field/enum.IrreducablePolynomial.html)

`IrreducablePolynomial`[trait. The](https://docs.rs/field/trait.Field.html)

`Field`[struct implements the](https://docs.rs/field/struct.GeneralField.html)

`GeneralField`[trait over all](https://docs.rs/field/trait.Field.html)

`Field`[s, even non-primitive ones. The](https://docs.rs/field/enum.IrreducablePolynomial.html)

`IrreducablePolynomial`[struct and implementation are specialized for primitive polynomials.](https://docs.rs/field/struct.PrimitivePolynomialField.html)

`PrimitivePolynomialField`Future releases of this crate will support optimized linear algebra primitives implemented across potentially heterogeneous compute environments.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use field::`- [IrreducablePolynomial](https://docs.rs/field/enum.IrreducablePolynomial.html);
- `pub use field::`- [Field](https://docs.rs/field/trait.Field.html);
- `pub use field::`- [GeneralField](https://docs.rs/field/struct.GeneralField.html);
- `pub use field::`- [PrimitivePolynomialField](https://docs.rs/field/struct.PrimitivePolynomialField.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [field](https://docs.rs/field/index.html)
- Implements arithmetic operations over all `GF(2^8)`extensions.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

To get you started quickly, the easiest and highest-level way to get
a random value is to use [ random()](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html); alternatively you can use

[. The](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)

`thread_rng()`[trait provides a useful API on all RNGs, while the](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[and](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)

`distributions`[modules provide further functionality on top of RNGs.](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)

`seq````
use rand::prelude::*;
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    // Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
    println!("char: {}", rand::random::<char>());
}
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let y: f64 = rng.gen(); // generates a float between 0 and 1
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

# reed_solomon_erasure - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/reed-solomon-erasure/^6.0/

## Expand description

This crate provides an encoder/decoder for Reed-Solomon erasure code.

Please note that erasure coding means errors are not directly detected or corrected, but missing data pieces (shards) can be reconstructed given that the configuration provides high enough redundancy.

You will have to implement error detection separately (e.g. via checksums) and simply leave out the corrupted shards when attempting to reconstruct the missing data.
